source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), Frontiers in Psychiatry article page opened through https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2019.00740 in my own browser tab: all sections, Tables 1 to 3 (Table 3 also read cell by cell from the page structure), author contributions, conflict-of-interest statement, editor and reviewer details, affiliations (the third read from the collapsed author list) and reference list; Figure 1 (PRISMA flow diagram) is an image and was not read for values; supplementary material not opened.

key_findings.note: Abstract › Methods: eight databases from inception to November 2018. Materials and Methods › Search Strategy: the four amphetamine keywords; same technique for ClinicalTrials.gov and grey literature. Results › Description of Studies: 643 titles, 604 removed on titles and abstracts, 39 screened, eight full articles, two excluded (reference 46, lithium and d-amphetamine in schizophrenia; reference 47, Sulaiman 2012 open-label aripiprazole study). See missed item 1: the per-source counts in the same paragraph add up to 838, not 643.

Table 2: every arm size, setting, country, age bound, duration and blinding comment as stated; arms sum to 314 (editors' sum recomputed); trials of 37 to 80 participants. Years from references 48 to 53.

Table 2: GRADE R+ for all six, with the note that low ratings came from small samples and design limitations; Jadad 4, 3, 4, 4, 3, 4 (four 4s, two 3s; Synthesis of Results, 1st paragraph, says about 67% scored 4). Risk of Bias in Included Studies, 1st paragraph: no trial at high risk of selection bias, two at high risk of performance and detection bias, none at risk of attrition or reporting bias.
Assessment of Heterogeneity and Data Synthesis and Analysis: data not combinable, heterogeneity not assessed, no cumulative meta-analysis.

key_findings.correction: 'Symptoms fell from baseline in both arms of every trial' is not stated for Verachai 2014: for that trial the review gives only the adjusted end-point comparison (no significant difference), the GEE result (quetiapine ahead) and time to cure (a slight difference favouring haloperidol, omitted from the finding). Within-arm reductions are stated for the other four head-to-head trials. Everything else matches.
key_findings.note: Results › Clinical Benefits, one paragraph per subsection; Table 3. The Farnia note (Table 3 labels the opposite of the text) is right.

key_findings.correction: The review gives mean CGI-S 2 on aripiprazole and 2.1 on placebo without a time point; 'at the end' is not in the text (Clinical Benefits › Aripiprazole, Placebo). The comparison with placebo ('decreased more ... than placebo') is from Table 3; the text gives p < 0.005 for aripiprazole reducing PANSS severity without naming the comparison. The rest matches: akathisia (AIMS) and agitation (BARS) higher and insomnia lower on aripiprazole (Side Effects › Aripiprazole, Placebo); higher dropout on aripiprazole on days 28 and 58 (Treatment Retention › Aripiprazole, Risperidone, last sentence).
key_findings.note: The card's note that a CGI-S of about 2 'at the end of the trial' shows little residual illness rests on the unstated time point; whichever time point it is, both arms were mildly ill then.

Side Effects (all subsections), Treatment Retention (all subsections), Table 3. Every Wang 2016 percentage fits 21 per arm (11, 4, 13, 6, 18, 6, 7 of 21; editors' arithmetic). Verachai completers 31 of 36 (86.11%) and 37 of 44 (84%) in the retention text. Leelahanaj somnolence 15.4% vs 7.4%, completers 93.1% vs 65.5%.
Limitations; Balancing Risk and Efficacy (longest trial 8 weeks, no follow-up after the trials); Consideration of the Use of Long-Acting Antipsychotics.

Discussion › Conclusions has four paragraphs; the 2nd (efficacious, may be self-limited), 3rd (clinically and ethically appropriate) and 4th (lacked placebo arms; unsure more placebo trials are needed) match.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed midpoints: Verachai 0.2914 with 0.1514 to 0.7341 gives 0.443 (−0.1514 gives 0.291); Farnia −1 with −1.6199 to 0.3801 gives −0.620 (upper −0.3801 gives −1.000); −0.7746 with −1.3806 to 0.1686 gives −0.606 (upper −0.1686 gives −0.7746). The other ten intervals are symmetric as printed.

Clinical Benefits › Aripiprazole, Risperidone (risperidone superior on hallucination, delusion, bizarre behaviour and thought disorder; aripiprazole on negative symptoms); Table 3 Farnia cells say the reverse; Summary of Main Findings says aripiprazole was better in two head-to-head trials.

The core issue stands (no comparison, time point or direction stated for any SMD). The Verachai example is weaker than written: the text reports no significant end-point difference after adjustment but also a GEE analysis in which quetiapine reduced symptoms more, and Table 3's label for 0.7602 ('quetiapine reduced PANSS score better') matches the GEE result. The Leelahanaj example (0.912, 0.3712 to 1.4528, labelled as end-point scores 'in both groups', beside p = 0.37) and the Samiei example (0.8895 labelled 'both drugs reduced') stand.

1 of 44 = 2.27%, 2 of 36 = 5.56%, 4 of 44 = 9.09%, 3 of 36 = 8.33%; with the labels as printed no whole count fits. Results text: haloperidol less hypotension and quetiapine more sedation; Summary of Main Findings: quetiapine more hypotension but less sedation.

4 of 26 = 15.38%, 1 of 26 = 3.85%, 2 of 26 = 7.69%, 2 of 27 = 7.41%; 27 of 29 = 93.10%, 19 of 29 = 65.52%. The retention subsection calls the trial 'olanzapine with risperidone'. The consequence's suggestion that side effects were counted among those who stayed does not fit the haloperidol arm (denominator 27, but 19 completers).

Recomputed from the 12 arm sizes in Table 2: mean 26.17, SD 7.61; mean per trial 314 / 6 = 52.3. For trials bounded at 18 to 60 a mean of 32 allows an SD of at most about 19.8, so 20.63 is implausible.

Table 3 Sulaiman row and footnote; text p < 0.005; days 28 and 58 in the text, 27 and 58 in the table; AIMS 26.6 vs 5.6, BARS 10.6 vs 5.6, SAS 10.6 vs 11.1. A firmer reason than the card's conditional: the 'dropout rate' falls from day 27 to day 58 in both arms (83% to 82%, 66% to 44%), which a cumulative dropout cannot do.

Abstract › Results ('with no adverse event'; no drug clinically superior); Treatment Retention › Haloperidol, Olanzapine (about one-third discontinued for extrapyramidal symptoms); Summary of Main Findings; Conclusions, 4th paragraph.

The text says 'about 85%', which 5 of 6 (83%) satisfies, so the share by itself is not impossible. The tension is with the same paragraph's two trials at high risk of performance and detection bias, which would leave at most 4 of 6 (67%) at low risk in every domain.

Reference 63 (Xue et al., Medicine (Baltimore) 2018, 97(8), e9786; a randomized trial of olanzapine and haloperidol in mental disorders induced by amphetamine-type stimulants) is cited in Discussion › Psycho-Pharmacological Characteristics, 1st paragraph, and is neither among the six included trials nor among the two exclusions (references 46 and 47).

Summary of Main Findings, 1st paragraph, against Treatment Retention › Aripiprazole, Risperidone (Wang lower retention; Farnia favoured aripiprazole) and Side Effects › Aripiprazole, Risperidone (Wang).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is the right instrument and critically low confidence follows from two critical flaws (item 2, no protocol; item 13, risk of bias not considered in the conclusions). I agree with every item; two could be argued more generously or more strictly without changing the overall: item 9 could be yes, since the Cochrane tool covers sequence generation, concealment, blinding and selective reporting (AMSTAR 2 rates the method, not whether per-trial results are in the main text); item 7 (yes) is generous given that a 2018 randomized trial cited in the discussion (Xue et al.) appears neither among the included nor among the excluded studies.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. Two corrections to the wording: (a) gap (3) says the Results show neither the discussion's 'aripiprazole better than risperidone in two trials' nor 'haloperidol superior to risperidone'; the first is right, but the Results text does state that haloperidol was superior to risperidone on hallucination, delusion and bizarre behaviour in weeks 1 to 3 (Clinical Benefits › Haloperidol, Risperidone); it is Table 3's intervals, all including zero, that do not support it (as the card's own key finding 4 says). (b) results_show says between-drug differences were 'mostly not significant in the trials' own analyses'; the review reports statistically significant item-level differences in Farnia 2014 (in both directions) and superiority in Wang 2016 (days 1 to 7) and Samiei 2016, and non-significance only for Verachai 2014 at the end point and Leelahanaj 2005. Suggested: 'between-drug differences varied in direction with the measure and time point, and the review's effect sizes cannot show which were significant'.

missed: Results › Description of Studies: the per-source counts (126, 70, 195, 164, 39, 2, 116, 77 and 49) add up to 838, not the 643 titles stated in the same sentence; no removal of duplicates is described (643 − 604 = 39 is consistent).
Verachai 2014: Table 3 says the cure rate slightly favoured quetiapine (SMD 0.2914), while the text says time to cure slightly favoured haloperidol (Clinical Benefits › Haloperidol, Quetiapine).
The CGI-S of 2 vs 2.1 in the placebo-controlled trial has no stated time point (key finding 5; anchor 14 of cl_meth_psychosis_treatment repeats 'at the end').
Exposure field: 'all oral' is stated by the review only for Sulaiman 2013 ('po'); the route is not given for the other five trials.
